question:
Choose the most suitable option to replace the highlighted part of the sentence.

 

Whom was the officer that you spoke to at the counter?
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. Who was the officer.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• "Whom" is the objective case. In this question the interrogative pronoun is the subject of "was the officer" — it stands for the person ("… was the officer?" = "He / She was the officer"). It must therefore be the nominative "Who".

◦ Corrected sentence: Who was the officer that you spoke to at the counter?

 

• "Who" is also the accepted form after the verb "be", because a pronoun that follows "be" is a complement of the subject and takes the nominative case.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1: "Who were the officer" — the case is fixed but the plural "were" does not agree with the singular "officer".

 

• Option 2: "Whom is the officer" — the objective "whom" is retained, and the tense is also changed.

 

• Option 3: No substitution required — incorrect, because "whom" cannot be the subject of the question.

 

NOTE

 

• "Whom" is used only as an object: Whom did you meet? (you met him). After the verb "be", use the nominative: Who is he?

question:
Find the part of the sentence that contains an error. If the sentence is free from error, select 'No error'.

 

People who live in glass houses (a)/ they should not throw stones (b)/ at others. (c)/ No error (d)
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. (b).

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The pronoun "they" is redundant. The subject — "People who live in glass houses" — is already stated, so repeating it with "they" creates a double subject. The pronoun must be removed.

◦ Corrected sentence: People who live in glass houses should not throw stones at others.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Part (a) is correct — "People who live in glass houses" is a complete subject with a proper relative clause ("who" for persons).

 

• Part (c) is correct — "at others" is a proper prepositional phrase.

 

• Option (d) No error — cannot be selected, because part (b) contains the redundant pronoun.

 

NOTE

 

• Never repeat the subject with a pronoun: Those who work hard they succeed (wrong); Those who work hard succeed (right). The proverb means that people with faults of their own should not criticise others.

question:
Find the part of the sentence that contains an error.

 

The Chief Guest, (a)/ Dr. Meera Nair, (b)/ she will inaugurate (c)/ the science exhibition tomorrow. (d)
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. (c).

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The subject of the sentence is "The Chief Guest, Dr. Meera Nair" — a noun followed by an appositive. Adding the pronoun "she" after it creates a double subject, which is ungrammatical. The pronoun must be removed.

◦ Corrected sentence: The Chief Guest, Dr. Meera Nair, will inaugurate the science exhibition tomorrow.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Part (a) is correct — "The Chief Guest," is a proper noun phrase acting as the subject.

 

• Part (b) is correct — "Dr. Meera Nair," is a proper appositive that identifies the subject and is set off by commas.

 

• Part (d) is correct — "the science exhibition tomorrow" is a proper object with a time adverb.

 

NOTE

 

• An appositive (words in commas that rename the noun) needs no pronoun after it: My brother, Rohit, he is a doctor (wrong) → My brother, Rohit, is a doctor (right).

question:
Find the part of the sentence that contains an error. If the sentence is free from error, select 'No error'.

 

The farmer and his bullocks (a)/ who had toiled together (b)/ were honoured at the fair. (c)/ No error (d)
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. (b).

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• When the antecedent includes both a person and an animal or thing, the relative pronoun must be "that". "Who" is used only for persons and "which" only for animals and things, so neither can refer to "the farmer and his bullocks" together.

◦ Corrected sentence: The farmer and his bullocks that had toiled together were honoured at the fair.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Part (a) is correct — "The farmer and his bullocks" is a proper compound subject.

 

• Part (c) is correct — the plural verb "were honoured" agrees with the compound subject, and the passive is properly formed.

 

• Option (d) No error — cannot be selected, because the relative pronoun in part (b) is wrong.

 

NOTE

 

• "That" is also preferred after superlatives and after all, any, only, no, the same, the very: All that glitters is not gold; He is the best player that I have seen.

question:
Find the part of the sentence that contains an error.

 

Nobody in the office (a)/ could tell me (b)/ that had actually (c)/ happened last night. (d)
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. (c).

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The clause needs a pronoun that means "the thing which" — a compound relative (interrogative) pronoun with no antecedent. That word is "what". "That" needs a noun antecedent before it (the thing that happened) and cannot introduce this noun clause.

◦ Corrected sentence: Nobody in the office could tell me what had actually happened last night.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Part (a) is correct — "Nobody in the office" is a proper singular subject.

 

• Part (b) is correct — "could tell me" is a proper modal verb with an indirect object.

 

• Part (d) is correct — "happened last night" correctly completes the past perfect "had actually happened" with a time adverb.

 

NOTE

 

• what = that which: I know what he did (no antecedent), but This is the thing that he did (antecedent "thing" present).

question:
Find the part of the sentence that contains an error. If the sentence is free from error, select 'No error'.

 

You may choose (a)/ that you like (b)/ from this collection. (c)/ No error (d)
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. (b).

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• "That" needs an antecedent noun before it. Here nothing precedes it, so the correct word is the compound relative pronoun "what" (= that which) or "whatever" / "whichever".

◦ Corrected sentence: You may choose whatever you like from this collection.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Part (a) is correct — "You may choose" is a proper modal + base verb construction.

 

• Part (c) is correct — "from this collection" is a proper prepositional phrase.

 

• Option (d) No error — cannot be selected, because "that" in part (b) has no antecedent.

 

NOTE

 

• what / whatever / whichever work without an antecedent: Take whatever you need. That / which need one: Take the book that you need.

question:
Choose the most suitable option to replace the highlighted part of the sentence.

 

The manager praised the staff for which they had achieved in the last quarter.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. for what they had achieved.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• When no antecedent noun stands before the pronoun, the compound relative pronoun "what" (= that which) is used. "For what they had achieved" means "for that which they had achieved". "Which" requires a noun antecedent (the results which they achieved), and there is none here.

◦ Corrected sentence: The manager praised the staff for what they had achieved in the last quarter.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 2: No improvement required — incorrect, because "which" has no antecedent.

 

• Option 3: "for that they had achieved" — "that" cannot follow a preposition to introduce this clause, and it also lacks an antecedent.

 

• Option 4: "for which they has achieved" — "which" is retained and "has" does not agree with the plural subject "they".

 

NOTE

 

• A relative clause without an antecedent begins with what: I am grateful for what you did; He gave me what I wanted.

question:
Find the part of the sentence that contains an error. If the sentence is free from error, select 'No error'.

 

He is the scientist (a)/ whom discovery (b)/ shook the world. (c)/ No error (d)
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. (b).

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The pronoun shows possession — "the scientist's discovery". The possessive relative pronoun required is "whose". "Whom" is objective and cannot stand before the noun "discovery".

◦ Corrected sentence: He is the scientist whose discovery shook the world.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Part (a) is correct — "He is the scientist" is a proper main clause.

 

• Part (c) is correct — "shook the world" is a proper predicate in the simple past, agreeing with "discovery".

 

• Option (d) No error — cannot be selected, because "whom" in part (b) is wrong.

 

NOTE

 

• whose = of whom / of which, used before a noun: a boy whose father is a pilot; a house whose roof leaks.

question:
Find the part of the sentence that contains an error.

 

The five sisters (a)/ never quarrel (b)/ and love (c)/ each other dearly. (d)
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. (d).

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• "Each other" is used for two persons or things, whereas "one another" is used for more than two. There are five sisters, so the reciprocal pronoun must be "one another".

◦ Corrected sentence: The five sisters never quarrel and love one another dearly.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Part (a) is correct — "The five sisters" is a proper plural subject.

 

• Part (b) is correct — the plural verb "never quarrel" agrees with the subject and is in the simple present.

 

• Part (c) is correct — "and love" is a properly parallel verb.

 

NOTE

 

• The two brothers help each other but All the members help one another. Also, a possessive form: each other's / one another's.

question:
Choose the most suitable option to replace the highlighted part of the sentence.

 

The examiner asked me who subject I had chosen for the optional paper.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. which subject.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• "Who" and "whom" are pronouns used for persons and cannot be placed before a noun. To ask about a choice of things, an interrogative adjective — "which" or "what" — must stand before the noun. So "which subject" is correct.

◦ Corrected sentence: The examiner asked me which subject I had chosen for the optional paper.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 2: "whom subject" — "whom" is a pronoun for persons and cannot qualify a noun.

 

• Option 3: "that subject" — a demonstrative, which does not create an indirect question and makes the sentence ungrammatical.

 

• Option 4: No substitution required — incorrect, because "who" cannot be followed by a noun.

 

NOTE

 

• Which is used for a limited choice (Which colour do you prefer — red or blue?), what for an open choice (What subject do you like?).

question:
Find the part of the sentence that contains an error. If the sentence is free from error, select 'No error'.

 

There are two paths (a)/ but I cannot decide who (b)/ of them leads to the village. (c)/ No error (d)
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. (b).

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• "Who" is used for persons, but "paths" are things. Moreover, when the choice is from a limited, known set (here, two paths), "which" is the correct interrogative pronoun.

◦ Corrected sentence: There are two paths but I cannot decide which of them leads to the village.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Part (a) is correct — "There are two paths" uses the plural verb "are" with the plural notional subject "paths".

 

• Part (c) is correct — the singular verb "leads" agrees with "which", and "to the village" is a proper prepositional phrase.

 

• Option (d) No error — cannot be selected, because "who" in part (b) is wrong.

 

NOTE

 

• Which of the two is taller? / Which of you knows the answer? — use "which of" for a limited group and "who" for an open group (Who wrote this book?).

question:
Find the part of the sentence that contains an error.

 

If one wants (a)/ to earn respect, (b)/ one should always (c)/ keep his promises. (d)
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. (d).

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The indefinite pronoun "one" must be followed by "one" or "one's" throughout the sentence. Switching to "his" is a person shift; the correct form is "one's promises".

◦ Corrected sentence: If one wants to earn respect, one should always keep one's promises.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Part (a) is correct — "If one wants" is a proper conditional clause with the singular verb "wants".

 

• Part (b) is correct — "to earn respect," is a proper infinitive phrase.

 

• Part (c) is correct — "one should always" continues the pattern correctly with "one".

 

NOTE

 

• One must respect one's elders (not "his" or "your" — SSC follows this traditional rule). Every student must bring his or her book is a different pattern.

question:
Choose the most suitable option to replace the highlighted part of the sentence.

 

One must learn to accept the consequences of what you do.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. what one does.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The subject of the sentence is the indefinite pronoun "one", so the later pronoun must also be "one". Shifting to "you" is a person shift and is treated as an error. Because "one" is singular, the verb must be "does".

◦ Corrected sentence: One must learn to accept the consequences of what one does.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 2: "what one do" — the pronoun is corrected but "do" does not agree with the singular "one".

 

• Option 3: "what he do" — "he" has no antecedent, and "do" does not agree with it either.

 

• Option 4: No substitution required — incorrect, because "you" creates a person shift from "one".

 

NOTE

 

• Keep the pronoun consistent: One should mind one's own business; You should mind your own business.

question:
Choose the most suitable option to replace the highlighted part of the sentence.

 

All the bulbs in the hall had fused, so we had to buy a new one.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. new ones.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The word "one" used as a substitute agrees in number with the noun it replaces. "Bulbs" is plural, so it must be replaced by the plural "ones". The article "a" cannot be used before a plural, so the correct form is "new ones".

◦ Corrected sentence: All the bulbs in the hall had fused, so we had to buy new ones.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 2: "a new ones" — the article "a" cannot be used with a plural word.

 

• Option 3: "the new one's" — "one's" is a possessive singular, which changes the sense and is grammatically wrong.

 

• Option 4: No improvement required — incorrect, because the singular "one" does not agree with the plural "bulbs".

 

NOTE

 

• I like this pen but not those ones; My shoes are old, so I need new ones. The plural of the substitute "one" is "ones"; "one's" is the possessive.

question:
Find the part of the sentence that contains an error.

 

The doctor felt (a)/ that there was important (b)/ to take complete rest (c)/ for at least a week. (d)
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. (b).

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The sentence needs an anticipatory (preparatory) "it" as a dummy subject for the infinitive phrase "to take complete rest". "There" is used only to state the existence of something (There is a book on the table), not to introduce an infinitive. So "there was important" must be "it was important".

◦ Corrected sentence: The doctor felt that it was important to take complete rest for at least a week.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Part (a) is correct — "The doctor felt" is a proper subject and verb in the simple past.

 

• Part (c) is correct — "to take complete rest" is a proper infinitive phrase.

 

• Part (d) is correct — "for at least a week" is a proper adverbial of duration.

 

NOTE

 

• It is essential to work hard, It is easy to make mistakes (it + adjective + infinitive) but There is a mistake in this sum (existence).

question:
Find the part of the sentence that contains an error. If the sentence is free from error, select 'No error'.

 

It was them (a)/ who reported the matter (b)/ to the police. (c)/ No error (d)
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. (a).

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• In a sentence of the pattern "It is / was + pronoun + who ...", the pronoun after "be" is the complement of the subject and must be in the nominative case. So "them" is wrong and the correct form is "they".

◦ Corrected sentence: It was they who reported the matter to the police.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Part (b) is correct — "who reported the matter" is a proper relative clause in the simple past.

 

• Part (c) is correct — "to the police" is a proper prepositional phrase.

 

• Option (d) No error — cannot be selected, because part (a) contains a wrong case.

 

NOTE

 

• It is I who am to blame, It was he who won, It is we who are responsible — nominative after be, and the verb after "who" agrees with the pronoun.

question:
Choose the most suitable option to replace the highlighted part of the sentence.

 

It is you who are responsible for the delay in the project.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. No improvement required.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The underlined part is already correct. In the pattern "It is + pronoun + who + verb", the pronoun after "be" is nominative ("you" has the same form in both cases), and the verb after "who" agrees with the antecedent pronoun — "you" takes "are".

◦ Sentence as given: It is you who are responsible for the delay in the project.

 

• "Who" is the correct relative pronoun because the antecedent "you" is a person.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1: "It is you who is" — "is" does not agree with the antecedent "you".

 

• Option 2: "It is your who are" — "your" is a possessive adjective that needs a noun after it, so it cannot follow "It is".

 

• Option 4: "It is you which are" — "which" is not used for persons.

 

NOTE

 

• The verb after "who" follows the person of the antecedent: It is I who am, It is he who is, It is they who are.

question:
Find the part of the sentence that contains an error.

 

Over the years, (a)/ there has been (b)/ many changes (c)/ in the city's skyline. (d)
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. (b).

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• In the "there + be" structure, the verb agrees with the real (notional) subject that follows it, not with "there". Here the real subject is the plural "many changes", so "there has been" must be "there have been".

◦ Corrected sentence: Over the years, there have been many changes in the city's skyline.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Part (a) is correct — "Over the years," is a proper introductory adverbial phrase.

 

• Part (c) is correct — "many changes" is a proper plural noun phrase, since "many" goes with plural countable nouns.

 

• Part (d) is correct — "in the city's skyline" is a proper prepositional phrase with the possessive.

 

NOTE

 

• There is a pen but There are two pens; There has been an increase but There have been many increases.

question:
Choose the most suitable option to replace the highlighted part of the sentence.

 

A lot of vacancies is there in the railways.
option_1: A lot of vacancies there is
option_2: There are a lot of vacancies
option_3: There is a lot of vacancies
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. There are a lot of vacancies.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• To state that something exists, English uses the introductory "There" + a form of "be", and the verb agrees with the noun that follows it. "A lot of vacancies" is plural, so the correct form is "There are a lot of vacancies". The given form "A lot of vacancies is there" is wrong in both structure and verb agreement.

◦ Corrected sentence: There are a lot of vacancies in the railways.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1: "A lot of vacancies there is" — the word order is unnatural and the singular "is" does not agree with the plural "vacancies".

 

• Option 3: "There is a lot of vacancies" — the structure is right but the singular "is" does not agree with the plural "vacancies".

 

• Option 4: No improvement required — incorrect, because "is" does not agree with "vacancies".

 

NOTE

 

• A lot of + plural noun → plural verb (There are a lot of books); a lot of + uncountable noun → singular verb (There is a lot of water).

question:
Choose the most suitable option to replace the highlighted part of the sentence.

 

Some of us prefer to work in the early hours of the day.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. No substitution required.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The underlined part is already correct. "Some of us" is a quantifier followed by a plural pronoun, and it takes the plural verb "prefer", which agrees with it.

◦ Sentence as given: Some of us prefer to work in the early hours of the day.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1: "Someone of us" — "someone" is a singular indefinite pronoun and is not used before "of us" like this; it would also not agree with "prefer".

 

• Option 2: "Some ones of us" — the plural "ones" is not used after "some" with "of us"; the phrase is unidiomatic.

 

• Option 4: "Somebody of us" — like "someone", it is singular and cannot be followed by "of us" in this sense.

 

NOTE

 

• Quantifier + of + plural pronoun is the correct pattern: Some of us, Many of us, Most of us, Few of us. Compounds like someone, somebody, everyone, anyone are not used before "of us / of them".

question:
Find the part of the sentence that contains an error. If the sentence is free from error, select 'No error'.

 

None (a)/ could solve the puzzle (b)/ except she. (c)/ No error (d)
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. (c).

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• "Except" is a preposition here, and a preposition is followed by the objective case. So "except she" is wrong and the correct form is "except her".

◦ Corrected sentence: None could solve the puzzle except her.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Part (a) is correct — "None" is a proper indefinite pronoun acting as the subject.

 

• Part (b) is correct — "could solve the puzzle" is a proper modal verb phrase with an object.

 

• Option (d) No error — cannot be selected, because part (c) uses the nominative case after a preposition.

 

NOTE

 

• But, except, save, besides, like — when used as prepositions — take the objective case: Nobody but me knew the secret; Everyone except them was present.

question:
Find the part of the sentence that contains an error.

 

The chairman as well as his advisers (a)/ was present at the function (b)/ and congratulated (c)/ themselves on the success of the plan. (d)
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. (d).

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• In phrases such as "as well as", "along with", "together with" and "in addition to", the noun that follows is not part of the subject. The main subject is "The chairman" (singular), and the verb "was" agrees with it. The reflexive pronoun must agree with the same subject, so it is "himself", not "themselves".

◦ Corrected sentence: The chairman as well as his advisers was present at the function and congratulated himself on the success of the plan.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Part (a) is correct — "The chairman as well as his advisers" keeps "chairman" as the main subject.

 

• Part (b) is correct — the singular verb "was" agrees with the main subject "chairman".

 

• Part (c) is correct — "and congratulated" is a proper past tense verb that continues the same subject.

 

NOTE

 

• The verb and the pronoun follow the first noun: The teacher, along with her students, has left her bag; The boys, together with their father, are here (the first noun "boys" is plural).

question:
Find the part of the sentence that contains an error. If the sentence is free from error, select 'No error'.

 

The teacher was upset about them (a)/ not submitting (b)/ the assignment on time. (c)/ No error (d)
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. (a).

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• A noun or pronoun that comes before a gerund ("submitting") should be in the possessive case, because it is the gerund (an action noun) that is the real object of the preposition. So "about them not submitting" must be "about their not submitting".

◦ Corrected sentence: The teacher was upset about their not submitting the assignment on time.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Part (b) is correct — "not submitting" is a properly negated gerund.

 

• Part (c) is correct — "the assignment on time" is a proper object with an adverbial phrase.

 

• Option (d) No error — cannot be selected, because part (a) uses the objective case before a gerund.

 

NOTE

 

• I do not like his shouting; She objected to my leaving early; We were surprised at your refusing — possessive before a gerund.

question:
Find the part of the sentence that contains an error.

 

During the picnic, (a)/ the children (b)/ enjoyed a lot (c)/ and played many games. (d)
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. (c).

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The verb "enjoy" needs an object. When no other object is stated, it takes a reflexive pronoun — "enjoy oneself". "Enjoyed a lot" lacks this object, so the correct form is "enjoyed themselves a lot".

◦ Corrected sentence: During the picnic, the children enjoyed themselves a lot and played many games.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Part (a) is correct — "During the picnic," is a proper introductory prepositional phrase.

 

• Part (b) is correct — "the children" is a proper plural subject.

 

• Part (d) is correct — "and played many games" is a proper parallel verb phrase in the simple past.

 

NOTE

 

• When "enjoy" has its own object, no reflexive pronoun is needed: She enjoyed the film but She enjoyed herself at the party. Other reflexive verbs: absent oneself from, apply oneself to, exert oneself, pride oneself on.

question:
Find the part of the sentence that contains an error. If the sentence is free from error, select 'No error'.

 

Do not pride on (a)/ your wealth, (b)/ for fortune is fickle. (c)/ No error (d)
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. (a).

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The verb "pride" is always used reflexively: "pride oneself on" something. Since the understood subject of the imperative is "you", the reflexive pronoun "yourself" must be inserted after "pride".

◦ Corrected sentence: Do not pride yourself on your wealth, for fortune is fickle.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Part (b) is correct — "your wealth," is a proper object phrase set off by a comma before the conjunction.

 

• Part (c) is correct — "for fortune is fickle" uses "for" correctly as a conjunction meaning "because".

 

• Option (d) No error — cannot be selected, because part (a) lacks the reflexive pronoun.

 

NOTE

 

• Reflexive-only verbs tested in SSC: pride oneself on, absent oneself from, apply oneself to, exert oneself, acquit oneself.
